narrative: The model estimated a 52.5% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt, just over a coin-flip level of risk. That is not a certainty, but it was enough for your application to be rejected. The strongest factor was your Law School Admission Test score: at 32, it is below the 37.18 average among accepted students, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor. At 2.70 it is below the 3.23 average among accepted students, but in this model its influence leaned toward passing rather than failing. Your third-year class decile was the third most important factor; at 4.00 it is below the accepted-student average of about 5.8, yet it also worked in your favor in the model’s assessment. In effect, the test score was the clearest risk signal and outweighed the factors that leaned toward success, producing the slightly-above-half failure estimate that led to denial. Next, focus on what you can change. Prepare carefully and consider retaking the Law School Admission Test, since a higher score would directly address the most influential concern. Seek admissions or prelaw advising about whether a GPA addendum, additional coursework, or a stronger academic record could help. Apply to schools that review applicants holistically, and ask for feedback so your next application can show concrete evidence of bar-exam readiness.
